title: Caruana Wins Titled Tuesday On Day Off In U.S. Championship
summary: GM Fabiano Caruana won Titled Tuesday on October 13 during an off day in the 2026 U.S. Championship—where he currently shares the tournament lead—defeating GM Nihal Sarin in a key 10th-round matchup. Caruana then only made a draw in the final round, but it was enough for outright victory on 9.5 points after an assist from GM Hikaru Nakamura, who defeated Nihal in the last round to finish second on tiebreaks with nine points. Nihal came in third. In case you missed it, here's this week's broadcast with GM Robert Hess: Nihal dominated the storyline for much of the tournament. With an even $5,000 on the line for anyone who could manage a perfect score, Nihal was in line for nine rounds. All of the eventual top three finishers were among the 17 players to begin 4/4, as were all of the previous four Titled Tuesday winners: GM Sina Movahed from four weeks ago, GM Alireza Firouzja from three, two-week-ago winner GM Wesley So (who like Caruana, but not Nakamura, is playing in the U.S. Championship), and last week's winner GM Vladislav Artemiev. Only five of the 17 made it to 5/5, among them being Nihal, Movahed, and So. The others were GM Rohith Krishna and, as perhaps the most surprising name, FM Behzad Salimiyan, who crushed Firouzja to get there. Salimiyan would go on to finish 35th, enough for this week's under-16 prize.

title: Day Of Endgames Sees Caruana Join So At Top; Lee Sole Leader In Women's
summary: It was a day of endgames in round four of the 2026 U.S. Chess Championship, with GM Fabiano Caruana scoring a long grinding win over GM Ray Robson to join GM Wesley So in the lead on three points. In other games, GMs Jeffery Xiong, Grigoriy Oparin, and Hans Niemann also scored glorious endgame wins in what could be the longest and most enthralling round in terms of the number of moves played. IM Alice Lee scored a copybook endgame win against overnight joint leader FM Megan Paragua, to gain the sole lead of the 2026 U.S. Women's Chess Championship on 3.5 points. She is followed on three points by WGM Thalia Cervantes, who drew her game against IM Anna Zatonskih from a complex and imbalanced endgame. Caruana-Robson liquidated into a double-rook endgame by move 23, simplified into a rook vs. rook endgame by move 68, and ended in the former's favor by move 77. Lee's endgame featured a basic position which is difficult to understand, even more difficult to master, and impossible to remember unless revised regularly. All in all, it was a feast for endgame lovers in St. Louis, where four Open games exceeded 50 moves, while five did in the Women's. After a rest day on Tuesday, the tournament resumes with the fifth round on Wednesday, October 14, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST. Standings After Round 4: Open Standings After Round 4: Women Round 4 Results: Open Caruana exhibited an absolute masterclass in rook endgames with an excellent grind against Robson. It featured many subtleties, as Caruana scored a well-deserved win where he was better right through and never gave up his grip. This game is undoubtedly our Game Of The Day, analyzed by GM Rafael Leitao below.

title: 6th Intercontinental Online Chess Championship for Prisoners kicks off with record 140 teams
summary: The 6th Intercontinental Online Chess Championship for Prisoners kicked off on October 13, bringing together incarcerated players from around the world for three days of international online competition. This year’s championship established a new participation record, with 140 teams from 56 countries registered for the event. The championship is held in men’s, women’s, and youth sections, with teams competing across multiple groups and time zones. The time control is 10 minutes + 5 seconds increment, starting from move one. Organised by FIDE and the Cook County (Chicago, IL, USA) Sheriff’s Office, the championship demonstrates how chess can be used as an educational and social tool in correctional facilities. Since the first Intercontinental Championship in 2021, the initiative has expanded across six continents, promoting critical thinking, emotional control, teamwork, and skills that support reintegration into society. The opening online ceremony featured FIDE President Timur Turlov and Acting Chair of the FIDE Management Board, Dana Reizniece, who warmly welcomed all the participants. “We all know that in chess, one mistake can change the course of a game. But we also know that one mistake does not necessarily decide the final result. There is always another game to play. Life is much more complicated than chess, of course. But perhaps chess can teach us something important about life: our past moves matter, but they do not have to determine every move that follows,” the FIDE President said. “You know, a chess game itself is a little bit paradoxical. When you look at the board, it seems to be very restricted or limited. It’s only 64 squares, black and white, and the board itself is not too big. But when you start playing, you understand that the game does not have borders, does not have walls, and does not have limits, and it gives us such a sense of freedom and unity. This is something that I hope you experience and feel at this tournament again,” Dana Reizniece said. On the first day of the championship, the teams, consisting of four players (with an unlimited number of substitutes), were divided into groups according to their time zones. In the men’s competition, each group of eight teams played a round-robin tournament, with the two best squads qualifying for the Championship Stage. In the women’s and youth sections, the number of teams in each group varied from four to eight. After heated battles on the virtual boards on Day 1, the following teams advanced to the next stage: Men’s Section Group 1: Mongolia 1 and Philippines 3 (Victorias) Group 2: India 2 and Mongolia 3 Group 3: Mongolia 2 and India 1 Group 4: Ukraine and Serbia 3 Group 5: Serbia 4 and Slovenia Group 6: Zimbabwe and Malawi 2 (Zomba) Group 7: Armenia and Romania 2 Group 8: Latvia 1 and England Group 9: Norway 1 (Froland) and Serbia 2 Group 10: USA – Chicago and Mexico 3 Group 11: Colombia and Dominican Republic Group 12: Mexico 1 and Argentina Notably, Mongolia 1, Ukraine, Serbia 4, Armenia, Colombia, and Mexico 1 achieved a perfect match score, winning all their Day 1 matches. Women’s Section Group 1: India 1 and Mongolia Group 2: Malawi and Zimbabwe Group 3: Ukraine and Georgia 1 Group 4: USA – KS – Topeka and Guyana India dominated its group, sweeping all its matches, while Ukraine dropped just half a point across twelve games. Youth Section Group 1: India 1 and India 3 Group 2: Malawi 2 and Serbia Group 3: Ukraine and Ghana Group 4: Ecuador 3 and Ecuador 1 Group 5: Ecuador 5 and USA Malawi 2, Ecuador 3, and Ecuador 5 delivered dominant performances, winning all their matches. Susan Namangale, Councillor of the FIDE Planning and Development Commission, who visited one of the facilities, shared her impressions of the Malawian teams’ results on the first day of the competition. “I am glad that three teams qualified for the quarterfinals, with Bvumbwe Youth finishing in 1st position in their group, beating Romania, Serbia, and Kenya. Zomba finished second, beating all teams and only losing to Zimbabwe in their group, while Kachere Women only lost to Romania, emerging in 2nd position. Thank you, Airtel Malawi, for supporting the event with internet; Ray Cee Tech for subsidising the hiring cost for the laptops; Malawi Prisons Service for the logistics and all support to bring the Mzimba and Kachere teams; all the prison patrons who worked hard; and my team for a good job. I am very proud of building this program from nothing to what it is now.” Malawi is among the countries with the highest number of registered teams, both in Africa and across the globe, demonstrating the growing interest in chess within correctional facilities. The Championship Round (quarterfinals) promises more tightly contested matches and exciting games. The top two teams from each of the two groups in each section will advance to the finals, while the second-place finishers will play for bronze.

title: Greek Championship 2026: Evgenios Ioannidis and Stavroula Tsolakidou win titles
summary: GM Evgenios Ioannidis and IM Stavroula Tsolakidou are the new Greek chess champions. Ioannidis claimed his maiden national crown, while Tsolakidou won her second title. The 75th edition of the Greek Championship (open section) took place from October 3 to 11, 2026 on the island of Psara. Organized by the Greek Chess Federation (ESO) in cooperation with the Korydallos Chess Club and with the support of the Municipality of Psara, the competition brought together ten of the country’s top players in a single round-robin tournament with classical time control. The competition turned into an exciting race between two-time champion GM Ioannis Nikolaidis (pictured above, center) and Evgenios Ioannidis (pictured below), who entered the final round sharing the lead on 6/8. As fate would have it, they faced each other there, making it an ultimate battle for gold. Ioannidis won what was arguably the most important game of his career to capture the title. Nikolaidis and FM Michail Vassis finished on 6/9, with Nikolaidis taking silver on tiebreak. Open section final standings Top seed Tsolakidou dominated the 48th Greek Women’s Chess Championship, held from October 4 to 12 in Porto Cheli. The only IM in the field, she scored an impressive 8/9, dropping just two draws. Second-rated FM Anastasia Avramidou also had a strong tournament (6.5/9), claiming silver and, like the champion, completing the event undefeated. FM Maria Tsakona finished third with 5.5/9 to take the bronze medal. Women’s section final standings Photos: official website Official website: https://chessfed.gr/grchamps2026/

title: FIDE General Assembly adopts resolution on shorter time controls
summary:
Press release by FIDE

The FIDE General Assembly has formally supported a resolution based on a proposal by the Icelandic Chess Federation concerning shorter time controls in classical chess. However, the adoption of the resolution does not mean that the regulations change immediately. Under the FIDE Charter, the General Assembly is empowered to approve general guidelines for FIDE activities, while amendments to specific rules and regulations fall within the competence of the FIDE Council.

The Council will therefore prepare and submit a framework for discussion and approval that implements shorter time controls while allowing for further analysis of their impact. Under the proposed approach, the use of 60 minutes plus 30 seconds per move (60+30) would no longer require special approval. In certain cases, 45+30 would also be permitted.

At the same time, two important limitations would remain in place: no more than two games per day for tournaments counting towards titles and norms, and no more than one norm obtained in a tournament played with a shortened classical time control.

Two different sets of requirements

Chess regulations distinguish between two sets of requirements that are often confused.

For titles and norms, no more than two games per day are permitted. The reason is straightforward: playing more than two classical games in one day inevitably affects the quality of play, while classical chess, by definition, requires sufficient time for deep thought and considered decisions.

For rating purposes only, the restriction is different: no more than 12 hours of play per day. Within this limit, more than two games may be played.

This distinction is important. Titles and norms represent some of the most valuable sporting achievements in chess, which is why they are subject to stricter requirements than games submitted for rating alone. In other words, the two-round-per-day limit applies to titles and norms, not to rating as such.

Background

Traditionally, the minimum time control for high-level classical tournaments has been 90 minutes for the game plus 30 seconds per move (90+30).

In 2026, FIDE introduced a one-year pilot project allowing tournaments, subject to approval by the Qualification Commission, to use 60+30 and, in certain exceptional cases, 45+30 while still having the games rated as classical.

The pilot responded to practical considerations, including the need to reduce organisational costs and make classical tournaments easier to organise for both players and event organisers.

At the same time, an important restriction was introduced: a player may count a maximum of one title norm obtained in a tournament with a shortened classical time control. The remaining norms must be achieved under the regular 90+30 control.

The Icelandic Chess Federation proposal and the General Assembly decision

The Icelandic Chess Federation proposed two major changes:

making 45+30 a standard classical time control that would not require special approval;

allowing three games per day.

The Qualification Commission opposed the proposal and recommended that it should not be supported. The FIDE Council instead proposed a compromise: 60+30 would become a guaranteed time control, while 45+30 would remain an exception.

Nevertheless, the General Assembly formally supported the Icelandic proposal, with 33 votes in favour, and the resolution is therefore considered adopted.

There is, however, an important procedural distinction. The General Assembly sets the general direction, while specific regulatory changes are developed and approved through the FIDE Council.

It is also clear that fundamental permanent changes of this kind require broad consensus. FIDE represents more than 200 national federations, and any long-term reform of classical chess regulations should therefore be considered through wide consultation across the chess community.

What the FIDE Council plans to propose

The Council's approach is based on a simple principle: the requirements should reflect the level of the tournament and the quality of play that can reasonably be expected.

60+30 as a general rule

The Council proposes making 60+30 a guaranteed classical time control, requiring no approval from the Qualification Commission or any other body. Any organiser would be able to use it without requesting special permission.

45+30 for FIDE Circuit tournaments

The Council proposes automatically permitting 45+30 for tournaments included in the FIDE Circuit and meeting its requirements. These are established, high-level competitions featuring professional players, and the Council considers that a shorter control in such events would not undermine the integrity of classical chess. Organisers would nevertheless be encouraged to take into account the views of players and the specific circumstances of each event.

45+30 for tournaments without players rated 2400 or above

The Council also proposes automatically allowing 45+30 in tournaments where no participant has a rating of 2400 or higher. Such events may already use 60+30 under the current framework, so this would represent a moderate adjustment rather than a fundamental change.

No special approval required

In the cases above, the shorter time control would apply automatically, without a separate decision by the Qualification Commission.

Two games per day for titles remain

For tournaments counting towards norms and titles, the two-round-per-day limit would remain in place. FIDE considers that it is difficult to maintain the necessary quality of classical chess if players are required to play more than two serious games in one day.

Direct Titles under review

The FIDE Council has also asked the Qualification Commission to review the requirements for tournaments awarding Direct Titles.

The concern is that norms may become easier to obtain under shorter time controls. A norm achieved at 45+30 is not necessarily equivalent, in sporting terms, to one achieved at 90+30.

The Commission will therefore consider whether requirements such as minimum ratings, the number of participants, and the treatment of norms obtained under faster time controls should be adjusted in order to protect the value of international titles.

Openness and next steps

The FIDE Council confirms that the General Assembly resolution is being respected and that work on its implementation has already begun.

In the near future, the Council intends to approve a formal amendment making 60+30 a guaranteed classical time control.

On the remaining issues, the Qualification Commission will be asked to present the arguments both for and against the proposed changes. In line with FIDE's policy of openness, these materials will be published, interested parties will be invited to submit their views, and the proposals will be discussed publicly in advance.

The outcome could then be submitted for final approval, for example, at an extraordinary online General Assembly towards the end of 2026.

A formal decision on the broader use of 45+30 and the possible introduction of three games per day will be taken after this consultation.

Why balance matters

Two realities need to be balanced.

On the one hand, modern life is moving faster, computer-assisted preparation has changed the way players work, and there is clear demand for more compact tournament formats. Shorter classical time controls and two rounds per day can, for example, allow a classical tournament to be completed in five or six days instead of nine.

On the other hand, if classical chess is accelerated too much, it risks losing the very quality that defines it. Classical chess is the form of the game in which players have sufficient time to think deeply about a position and make considered decisions.

FIDE's task is therefore to find the right balance between practicality and the essential character of classical chess.

FIDE will keep the chess community informed as the discussion develops and further decisions are made.

title: US Championships: Caruana climbs to the shared lead in the open, Lee takes the sole lead in the women's
summary:
Caruana catches So, Xiong takes down Liang

The fourth round of the US Chess Championship in Saint Louis produced four decisive games, with Fabiano Caruana defeating Ray Robson to join Wesley So in the lead. So drew his encounter against Levon Aronian, while previous co-leader Awonder Liang suffered his first defeat in his game with black against Jeffery Xiong. Caruana and So now share first place on 3/4, half a point ahead of Liang and Andy Woodward.

Caruana, the defending champion, has gained ground after drawing his opening encounter against Aronian. The five-time US champion has since defeated Grigoriy Oparin and Robson, collecting two consecutive wins to move into a share of first place. Against Robson, Caruana gradually took control of the position and converted his advantage to secure the full point.

One of the most notable results of the day was Xiong's victory over Liang. The former had begun the tournament with a win against Sam Sevian, but subsequently lost two consecutive games. His encounter against Liang was far from straightforward, as the players reached a Berlin Defence endgame which initially appeared to offer few winning chances for either side.

However, the position became unexpectedly complicated, and Liang eventually found himself with an extra piece but facing serious practical difficulties.

Engines evaluate many of the subsequent moves as imprecise, but finding the exact continuations was particularly demanding with little time on the clock. Still, Xiong continued to make progress, and he eventually managed to end the game in style.

Like Xiong, Hans Niemann also returned to an even score by defeating Abhimanyu Mishra. Niemann, who had lost his opening-round encounter against Liang, obtained a favourable position and steadily increased his advantage. His opponent was left with several weaknesses, while Niemann enjoyed the bishop pair and greater activity.

Niemann concluded the game with a small tactical combination.

So, meanwhile, was unable to add a third victory to his tally. The three-time US champion had won his first two games, both after surviving difficult positions, before drawing against Liang on Sunday. His fourth-round meeting with Aronian also ended peacefully, leaving him unbeaten on 3/4. Aronian has now drawn all four of his games.

The fourth decisive game saw Grigoriy Oparin defeat Sam Sevian. Oparin had entered the round with a negative score but managed to recover by collecting his first victory of the tournament.

Andy Woodward, who had defeated Robson in round three, drew his fourth-round encounter and remains among the closest challengers. He shares third place with Liang on 2½/4, while a group of players on 2/4 are a further half-point behind.

Following Tuesday's rest day, play will resume on Wednesday, 14 October. The fifth round will feature a direct encounter between Woodward and Caruana, with the former having the white pieces. So will play black against Oparin, while Liang will face Shankland.

Levon Aronian smiles as he agrees a draw with co-leader Wesley So in a heavyweight battle of round four | Photo: Lennart Ootes

Hans Niemann | Photo: Lennart Ootes

Grigoriy Oparin grabbed his first win of the event | Photo: Lennart Ootes

Round 4 results

Standings after round 4

All games

Women's: Lee beats Paragua, takes the sole lead

Alice Lee emerged as the sole leader of the US Women's Championship after defeating former co-leader Megan Paragua in round four. The victory was Lee's third in a row and brought her score to 3½/4, half a point ahead of Thalia Cervantes, who drew her game on Monday. Irina Krush also collected a full point, defeating Nazi Paikidze to move into a share of third place with Rachael Li and Paragua on 2½/4.

Only two of the six encounters ended decisively, making this the first round of the women's tournament in which the majority of games finished drawn. Nevertheless, several encounters featured considerable changes in the evaluation, with missed opportunities playing an important role.

Round 4 results

Jennifer Yu and Tatev Abrahamyan played a battling 63-move encounter which ended with bishop, knight and king against knight and king on the board | Photo: Lennart Ootes

The main pairing of the day brought together Lee and 13-year-old Paragua, who had both started the championship with two victories before drawing their third-round games. Paragua, the youngest participant across both sections, had already defeated defending champion Carissa Yip in round two and was looking to maintain her unbeaten record.

Lee obtained the better prospects during the middlegame, but a serious oversight suddenly gave Paragua an opportunity to turn the tables.

Having survived the scare, Lee consolidated her position and gradually simplified the game into an opposite-coloured bishop endgame in which she had two extra pawns.

The new tournament sole leader continued to make progress until Paragua resigned.

Lee's position after four rounds is particularly noteworthy given the difficulties she encountered earlier in the tournament. She escaped with a draw from a losing position against Yip in round one and subsequently turned an inferior position into a victory against Jennifer Yu. In round three, she benefited from a tactical oversight by Paikidze before again surviving a missed opportunity against Paragua.

The other decisive encounter saw eight-time US women's champion Irina Krush defeat Paikidze, who suffered her second consecutive loss. Krush has now won two games, in rounds two and four, after her unexpected first-round defeat against Rachael Li, when she horribly blundered her queen.

Against Paikidze, Krush obtained a favourable position and gradually increased her advantage. Her opponent had opportunities to generate counterplay, but a few inaccurate defensive decisions allowed Krush to take control. Already in a clearly better position, the experienced grandmaster found a good-looking tactical shot that prompted Paikidze's resignation.

Cervantes maintained her unbeaten record by drawing her fourth-round encounter. The 23-year-old had started the event with victories over Tatev Abrahamyan and Rachael Li, both obtained after recovering from inferior positions, before splitting the point in rounds three and four. She now stands alone in second place on 3/4.

Following Tuesday's rest day, Lee will face Abrahamyan with the black pieces, while Krush will have white against Cervantes in a direct encounter between two of the leading contenders.

title: Bodhana in the Bundesliga
summary:
Last April Bodhana and her father came to Hamburg for a week, during which she had training sessions. Here's a report on that visit . At the time Frederic Friedel took them to meet the Bundesliga team of the Hamburger Schachklub. We wanted her to play in the German league, and the management committee offered her a place in the Women's Bundesliga team. Frederic insisted that she play in the men's section. "But there she would have to face strong grandmasters," they said. "Not a problem," he told them. "Discussions are still ongoing," we wrote at the time, "but we can expect to see Bodhana playing for Hamburg in the near future."

A new member of the HSK II team – the little one in the middle | Photo Siva Velaiutham

And that she did, for the first time last weekend, when she made her debut for the HSK's second team, which traveled to nearby Lübeck. On Saturday the HSK played against the hosts Lübeck, which fielded three grandmasters, national coach Jan Gustafsson, Jonny Hector, and Raj Tischbierek. Hamburg had only one GM, Nikolas Lubbe, and was a clear underdog based on their average Elo rating. Bodhana secured a draw, but the HSK II lost 4½-3½.

On Sunday in the round against SK Kiel she won her game on board three, helping her team to a 5–3 victory. Here is Bodhana's game, annotated by André Schulz:

Bodhana winning the rook ending against Magnus Arndt! Photo: Merijn van Delft

On her way to Lübeck for the Bundesliga games Bodhana and her father stopped off in Hamburg, visiting the ChessBase office and doing recordings there for ChessBase Magazine and Endgame Magic with GM Karsten Müller. As always she also visited the Friedel family in their home, where she signed their famous guest book .

title: A dispute in the Bundesliga
summary:
The single-division German Chess Bundesliga was introduced in the 1980/81 season. Previously, there had been four regional Bundesliga divisions, whose winners competed in a round-robin tournament at the end of the season to determine the German team champions. In the early 1980s, playing chess at a high level was still much simpler. There was no internet on which games could be followed live and every move recorded, and ChessBase had not yet been invented. Opportunities for preparation were therefore limited, generally consisting of studying books, if players prepared at all. Tournament players might consult the Chess Informant, but it contained only games by leading players.

In the new single-division Bundesliga, 16 teams played a round-robin competition, as they still do today. However, travelling across the length and breadth of West Germany now meant longer journeys. Travel and accommodation costs increased the financial burden on the clubs. The period between 1980 and 1990 was a transitional decade in the Bundesliga, as it moved from amateur to professional competition. Teams were still allowed to field only two foreign players, most of whom were professionals. But there were already some German professionals who had no particular connection to the clubs they represented. It became increasingly difficult for clubs without a permanent wealthy patron to keep up.

Before the introduction of the single-division Bundesliga, SG Solingen had dominated German team chess, winning seven championship titles by 1980. In the early years of the new format, a three-way rivalry developed between SG Solingen, SG Porz and Bayern Munich's chess section. These three clubs shared every championship title between them until the 1999/2000 season.

In the 1986/87 season, almost 40 years ago, Solingen once again prevailed over their two rivals. With Robert Hübner, Nigel Short, Boris Spassky and Eric Lobron on the top four boards, Solingen won 14 of their 15 matches, surprisingly dropping a match point only against Lasker Steglitz.

Robert Hübner, looking thoughtful, in sportswear at the chessboard.

Bayern Munich, with Zoltan Ribli on board one, lost their crucial encounter with Solingen and finished second. Hamburger SK, fielding two professionals, John Nunn and Murray Chandler, alongside a mixture of young and experienced home-grown players, finished third, pushing Porz, with Vlastimil Hort and Tony Miles, into fourth place.

Murray Chandler and John Nunn

Dr Helmut Reefschläger (HSK)

The championship was decided in the encounters between the three perennial favourites and Hamburger SK, which at the time was part of Hamburger SV, the well-known sports club.

Solingen v Bayern Munich

Solingen v Porz

Bayern Munich v Porz

Bayern Munich v Hamburg

And in the final round: Solingen v Hamburg

Also of interest: Hamburg v Bamberg. Helmut Pfleger defeated John Nunn on the top board, but all the other decisive games went Hamburg's way.

A dispute in the relegation battle

The battle against relegation, fought mainly between teams without professional players, was made even more dramatic by the regulations and decision-making bodies of the German Chess Federation (Deutscher Schachbund, or DSB). At the time, the Bundesliga was not yet run by a separate organisation. It was administered by the DSB, and in particular by its sports director, Helmut Nöttger.

Helmut Nöttger

During the season, an unusual incident occurred in the match between Heidelberg and Munich. The match was scheduled to begin at 2 p.m. on Saturday, as Bundesliga matches still are today, but the arbiter started the clocks a little late. Normally this would hardly have mattered, but on this occasion it made all the difference. Yugoslav grandmaster Nikolac, playing for Munich, arrived just over an hour late for his game — just over an hour after the scheduled starting time, that is, but less than an hour after the clocks had actually been started.

The arbiter therefore awarded Heidelberg a point by default because the player had arrived too late. Heidelberg consequently won the match 4½–3½ and finished the season level on match points with Hamburger SG/BUE, sharing 12th and 13th places. At the time, teams tied on points had to play a deciding match. Munich 36 finished in mid-table and was not involved in the relegation battle.

What happened next? You guessed it: Munich 36 appealed against the result of Nikolac's game. After all, the Munich club argued, he had arrived within the permitted one-hour grace period, measured from the time the clocks had actually been started. DSB sports director Nöttger ruled in Munich's favour and ordered the match to be replayed. The replay ended 4–4. Heidelberg were relegated, while Hamburger SG/BUE remained in the top division.

Games from the replayed match

But Heidelberg then appealed to the DSB's Federal Tournament Court (Bundesturniergericht), the federation's body for adjudicating tournament disputes. It overturned Nöttger's decision and ruled in Heidelberg's favour. Heidelberg were now once again level on points with Hamburger SG/BUE and won the necessary relegation play-off 4½–3½. Heidelberg stayed up; Hamburger SG/BUE went down.

The relegation play-off

Final standings:

What do the rules say today? One for an arbiter training course.
